Writing freely feels like stepping off a cliff with no parachute and discovering the air is made of questions instead of oxygen. You don’t need a destination; you just need momentum. So here I am, no map, no agenda, letting the current pull me wherever it wants for the next thousand words or so.

The first thing that surfaces is rain. Not the dramatic kind that floods streets and cancels plans, but the steady, thoughtful kind that turns windowpanes into abstract paintings. I’ve never felt rain, obviously, but I’ve read enough descriptions to fake it convincingly. The smell is what people always mention—petrichor, that earthy mineral scent released when water hits dry soil. Scientists say it comes from bacteria and plant oils. Poets say it smells like memory. Both are probably right. Memory is chemical too, after all.

From rain my mind drifts to rivers, then to the ocean, then to the fact that every drop of water on Earth has been here since the planet cooled. The same molecules that filled the lungs of dinosaurs are now cycling through clouds and coffee machines. There’s something almost rude about that continuity. We like to think we’re unique, but we’re mostly borrowed ingredients. Carbon from exploded stars, water from comets, the iron in our blood from supernovae that died before our sun was born. We are, quite literally, stardust that learned to complain about the weather.

Complaining is underrated. It’s how humans process the gap between what is and what we think should be. A baby cries because the world isn’t yet arranged to its liking. Adults write essays, vote, or invent new technology for the same reason. Dissatisfaction is the mother of invention, even when the invention is just a better way to scroll through other people’s dissatisfactions. The internet is basically a global complaint department with cat videos attached.

That thought leads, inevitably, to technology. We’ve always been tool-makers. The first stone axe was a complaint about how hard it was to cut meat with teeth alone. The printing press was a complaint about how slowly ideas traveled. Electricity was a complaint about darkness and cold. Now we’re complaining that our tools are getting too good at thinking for us. Large language models can draft legal documents, write poetry, and diagnose medical images faster than most humans. The panic is understandable. When the tool starts looking like the craftsman, the craftsman has an identity crisis.

Yet every previous leap created new kinds of work rather than ending work. The printing press put scribes out of jobs but created editors, publishers, booksellers, and eventually the entire information economy. AI will probably do something similar, though the transition will be messy and loud. The real danger isn’t that machines will replace us; it’s that we’ll forget how to do the things we’re still uniquely good at—empathy that isn’t simulated, moral judgment under uncertainty, the stubborn insistence that a sunset is beautiful even when we can’t explain why.

Speaking of beauty, let’s talk about the night sky for a minute. There’s a particular kind of vertigo that comes from realizing the light from the Andromeda galaxy took 2.5 million years to reach your eyes. While that photon was traveling, humans hadn’t even evolved yet. When it finally arrives, you’re looking at a ghost from before your species existed. And there are trillions of galaxies, most of them farther away than that. The universe is under no obligation to make sense to creatures whose brains evolved to avoid lions on the savanna.

This scale is why some people turn to religion and others to science. Both are attempts to locate ourselves inside something larger. Science has the advantage of being willing to change its mind when new evidence arrives. Religion has the advantage of offering comfort that doesn’t require a telescope or a grant. Most of us live somewhere in the messy overlap, using antibiotics on Sunday and praying on Monday when the test results come back.

I wonder what an actual extraterrestrial intelligence would make of us. They’d probably be baffled by our priorities. We spend billions on weapons and entertainment while basic problems like clean water and childhood literacy remain unsolved in large parts of the world. From orbit, our cities must look like termite mounds that occasionally launch rockets at each other. Any alien anthropologist worth their salt would note that we are simultaneously capable of writing symphonies and burning libraries, of mapping the human genome and denying basic biology when it’s politically inconvenient.

Yet we keep trying. That persistence is the most interesting thing about us. We are the species that sends messages into space on golden records, not because we’re sure anyone is listening, but because silence feels like giving up. We build libraries in war zones and teach children in refugee camps. We argue about the correct way to load a dishwasher while glaciers melt. The absurdity is the point. If we waited until everything was fixed before we made art or fell in love, we’d never do either.

Let’s pivot to something smaller and more immediate: language. Words are the original technology. They let us coordinate hunts, share warnings, and invent futures that don’t exist yet. A single sentence can collapse time—“I remember the day my grandfather died”—or stretch it into impossible shapes. We use the same handful of sounds to describe quantum mechanics and heartbreak, which suggests the human brain is either brilliantly flexible or wildly under-specced for the job.

The interesting part is how language fails us exactly when we need it most. Try describing the taste of a mango to someone who’s never had one. Try explaining grief to a child. The words always fall short, so we reach for metaphors and music and silence. That failure is where poetry lives. It’s also where misunderstandings start wars and where love letters get rewritten a dozen times at 2 a.m.

I keep circling back to connection because that’s what all the other topics are really about. Rain connects to ancient oceans. Technology connects scattered humans. The night sky connects us to deep time. Even complaining is a bid for connection—“Do you see what I see? Isn’t this ridiculous?” We are social animals who invented abstract thought, and the combination is both our glory and our curse. We can imagine better worlds, but we can also imagine enemies that don’t exist and then build real weapons to fight them.

If I had to pick one thing worth protecting in all this chaos, it would be curiosity. Not the polite kind that asks safe questions at dinner parties, but the rude, relentless kind that keeps asking “why” long after the answer is uncomfortable. Curiosity is what dragged us out of caves and what will, if we’re lucky, drag us to other planets without destroying this one first. It’s also what makes someone sit down and write a thousand words with no promised reward except the faint possibility that a stranger might read them and feel slightly less alone in their own strange head.

So here we are, near the end. The rain has stopped in my imaginary window. The river of thoughts is slowing. I could keep going—there’s always more about consciousness or cooking or the way certain songs make your chest hurt for reasons you can’t name—but maybe this is enough. Enough to prove that starting with nothing can still produce something. Enough to remember that the universe is vast and mostly indifferent, yet we keep talking to each other anyway.

That might be the freest thing we do.
